text:
A thousand requests arrive in the same second. Each one spends most of its time waiting: on a database, on another service. Serve them one after another, and the server sits idle through every wait while the queue grows. Serve them at once, and they start sharing things: a counter, a lock, a connection. That's where the bugs live. Sixteen questions on concurrency. Nine get a figure each, and seven go quickly at the end.

Question one. Concurrency versus parallelism, what is the difference? Concurrency is dealing with many tasks at once. One core switches between them, and each makes progress in turns. Parallelism is doing many at the same instant, which takes more than one core. So async code on one thread is concurrent, but not parallel. Processes spread across cores are both. The follow-up is what parallelism can buy. If five percent of the work can't be split, no number of cores makes it more than twenty times faster, and a hundred cores already get about seventeen. That's Amdahl's law.

Question two. Processes versus threads, how do they differ? Threads live inside one process and share its memory, so talking is cheap: one thread writes a value, another reads it. That sharing is also the danger. Two threads can corrupt the same state. Processes each get their own memory. A crash in one can't corrupt another, and they run truly in parallel. The price is talking: data passed between them has to be serialized through pipes or queues, and every process costs more memory.
